extracted.intended_audience: immigration attorneys, advocates, service providers, state and local benefits agencies, DHS/USCIS officers and rulemakers, and other stakeholders commenting on or implementing public charge policy
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory guidance and standards for applying the public charge ground of inadmissibility: what factors and types of benefits DHS will consider, how DHS will collect information, and recommended/required implementation actions (forms, outreach, training) to mitigate chilling effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory minimum factors to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 212(a)(4) of the INA requires DHS to consider how a noncitizen's age; health; family status; assets, resources, and financial status; and education and skills impact whether the noncitizen is likely at any time to become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These enumerated factors are the baseline inputs for public charge inadmissibility determinations; DHS will collect relevant information to evaluate them and consider them in a totality of circumstances assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of Support consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the statute, DHS may also consider an applicant's Affidavit of Support Under Section 213A of the INA, if applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The affidavit is an available piece of evidence that can be weighed along with the statutory minimum factors when relevant to the applicant's likelihood of becoming a public charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory definition of 'likely at any time to become a public charge'
rubrics_metrics.description: Define 'likely at any time to become a public charge' as likely at any time to become primarily dependent on the government for subsistence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linking the regulatory definition to the statutory text provides a clear connection and helps limit consideration to primary dependence rather than any incidental receipt of benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of public benefits to be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will consider 'public cash assistance for income maintenance' and 'long-term institutionalization at government expense,' and benefits referenced in 8 CFR 212.21(b) and (c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule establishes key regulatory definitions (e.g., 'public cash assistance for income maintenance', 'long-term institutionalization at government expense', 'receipt', 'government', 'household') to make determinations clearer and narrower than the 2019 Final Rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude certain benefits from consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not consider receipt of, or certification or approval for future receipt of, public benefits not referenced in 8 CFR 212.21(b) or (c), such as SNAP or other nutrition programs, Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP), Medicaid (other than for long-term institutional services under section 1905(a) of the Social Security Act), housing benefits, benefits related to immunizations or testing for communicable diseases, or other supplemental or special-purpose benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explicit exclusion aims to limit chilling effects by clarifying that many commonly used public programs (including immunizations, COVID-19 testing/treatment, SNAP, housing programs, and most Medicaid) will not be considered in public charge determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow consideration of past or current receipt of certain benefits as indicator of future dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS believes it is important to consider a noncitizen's past or current receipt of certain benefits, to the extent such receipt occurs, as it can be indicative of future primary dependence on the government for subsistence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While acknowledging chilling effects, DHS argues past/current receipt of some benefits may be probative of likely future dependence and therefore may be weighed in the adjudication where legally appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect necessary applicant information (household, income, assets, liabilities, education/skills, public cash assistance, long-term institutionalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS reviewed the Form I-485 and proposed additional questions regarding household size, income, assets, liabilities, an applicant's education or skills, an applicant's use of public cash assistance for income maintenance, and any long-term institutionalization of the applicant at government expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS will amend Form I-485 (rather than require a separate I-944) to collect only information related to public charge inadmissibility determinations and to reduce paperwork burdens; applicants not subject to section 212(a)(4) will be instructed to skip related questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize paperwork burden and avoid duplicative forms
rubrics_metrics.description: This rule ensures DHS collects information regarding each of the statutory minimum factors, but does not require any additional forms and imposes a comparatively smaller paperwork burden than the 2019 Final Rule's Form I-944.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS determined Form I-485, with some amendments, will sufficiently collect necessary information; additional space is provided if applicants need to provide more information; no unrelated evidence is requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include screening question to skip irrelevant questions
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS included a question asking applicants if they are subject to the public charge ground of inadmissibility and, if not, instructing that they may skip the subsequent related questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces burden on applicants not subject to section 212(a)(4) and avoids unnecessary collection of information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness, consistency, and evidence-informed adjudications
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will ensure public charge inadmissibility determinations will be fair, consistent with law, and informed by relevant data and evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule aims to produce fair and consistent adjudications to avoid unequal treatment of similarly situated individuals and to be grounded in empirical evidence to the extent available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary burdens on applicants, officers, and benefits-granting agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS intends the rule to avoid unnecessary burdens on applicants, officers, and benefits-granting agencies while mitigating chilling effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In contrast to the 2019 Final Rule, the final rule seeks to reduce complexity and time burdens for applicants and the workload on service providers and state agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer clear, simple, and prominently displayed explanations to reduce chilling effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters recommended beginning the final rule with a simply worded executive summary or prominently displayed simple and clear description of the limited circumstances in which noncitizens are and are not subject to a public charge assessment, and the effective date and process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS obliged by adding an executive summary and believes clear language and definitions reduce chilling effects and help both officers and the public understand applicability and limits of the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide explicit lists of benefits considered/not considered (prefer lists over technical definitions for public communication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters suggested that a list, rather than a technical definition, is more useful and comprehensible for those seeking to understand the scope of the public charge assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS added clarifying regulatory text and will plan outreach materials; commenters recommended multiple agencies publish annual letters clarifying which programs they administer are considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robust public communications and outreach (multilingual, multi-channel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters recommended DHS conduct a comprehensive information campaign, clearly communicate that the 2019 Final Rule is no longer in effect, list benefits that will be considered, and emphasize that no other benefits will be taken into account; materials should be available in multiple languages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS is planning a robust communication effort in conjunction with publication, and will coordinate with benefits-granting agencies and community partners; communications are not part of the rulemaking but will be implemented in follow-on guidance and outreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partner with benefit-granting agencies and provide sample materials for States
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters recommended that multiple government agencies draft letters distinguishing programs (e.g., SSI and TANF) and post them on DHS's public charge resource page, updated annually, and that DHS provide sample language for State and agency websites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such interagency coordination (while not part of the regulatory text) was recommended to reduce chilling effects and help service providers respond accurately to immigrant families' concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide streamlined mechanism for questions about benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters suggested DHS maintain a streamlined mechanism for submitting questions about benefits that may be considered in a public charge inadmissibility determination, to allow noncitizens to be more confident they can access listed programs without endangering immigration status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A central question/clarification mechanism would reduce calls to state programs and simplify training and communications for agencies serving immigrant communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund and coordinate with trusted community organizations for outreach
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters recommended DHS provide funding to trusted community organizations, including health and social services organizations, to provide outreach and education such as 'know your rights' presentations, hotlines, phone banks, social media engagement, and train-the-trainer sessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although new grant funding is outside the rulemaking's scope, DHS will take recommendations under advisement as it implements and monitors the rule; DHS itself intends to conduct robust outreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train and retrain immigration officers and caseworkers; publish policy guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters indicated DHS should invest significantly in training and retraining immigration officers and case workers; USCIS plans to issue policy guidance in its USCIS Policy Manual and to conduct training to ensure consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USCIS will provide officers with a solid foundation on public charge determinations and will issue policy guidance (including information from the NPRM and final rule) accessible to applicants, officers, and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly reassure that public health services and COVID-19-related care are not considered
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters asked for a clear, concise statement that receiving government-funded health care or insurance will never have negative immigration consequences; DHS reiterates it will not consider receipt of treatments or preventative services related to COVID-19, including vaccinations, in a public charge determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS has made clear in regulatory text and will reiterate in outreach and guidance that immunizations, testing, and treatment for communicable diseases are excluded from consideration (and will not be considered except for long-term institutionalization services noted elsewhere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not require data collection from schools
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commenters raised concerns about school districts forwarding household income information; DHS did not propose to collect any information from schools and such suggestions are outside the scope of the rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS notes this rule does not apply to deportability determinations and will not impose data collection requirements on schools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly protect children's benefit usage from being considered
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters urged DHS to clearly communicate that benefits received by children are not considered as part of any public charge inadmissibility determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS will emphasize in outreach that benefits received by children (and many family supports) are not considered, to reduce chilling effects that deter families from accessing child health, nutrition, or school supports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory and evidentiary limits tied to Congressional intent and precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS notes that Congress's prohibition on considering prior receipt of certain benefits for specific classes (e.g., 8 U.S.C. 1641(c)) indicates Congress understood and accepted consideration of past receipt of public benefits in other circumstances; DHS has never believed this requires consideration of all benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This legal rationale supports DHS's position that some past receipt may be considered where appropriate, but that statutory and regulatory limits constrain the scope of what may be weighed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid return to the 2019 Final Rule's complex, burdensome formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters criticized the 2019 Final Rule's layered, complex public charge formula and burdens such as Form I-944; DHS agrees that the 2019 Final Rule imposed burdens and states the new rule avoids unnecessary burdens and complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule favors clearer definitions, streamlined data collection, and totality-of-circumstances adjudication rather than a rigid, multi-factor formula that was difficult for applicants and service providers to understand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy should be consistent with nation's economic security and not impose undue barriers
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS has concluded this rule is consistent with the nation's economic security and will help ensure public charge determinations are fair and informed by relevant data and evidence, while not imposing undue barriers for noncitizens seeking admission or adjustment of status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule is framed as balancing enforcement of the statutory public charge ground with minimizing harms and chilling effects and ensuring administrative practicability.
